note_tweet.text:
Most AI agents can't keep quiet: what Deepnote's Agent Initiative Benchmark tells you about building a proactive agent

When a proactive agent should have stayed silent, the 12 frontier models in Deepnote's new benchmark held back only 6 times out of 10. When help was actually needed, they sent a message 9 times out of 10. That gap is the whole story of always-on agents right now, and it matters more for your design than which model tops the leaderboard.

Deepnote released the Agent Initiative Benchmark on November 13. It tests a job most agent evals ignore: an agent sits in a company Slack, decides on its own whether a conversation needs it, digs through other systems for evidence, then posts in the right place or says nothing.

How the benchmark works

Deepnote built a synthetic software company called PageMantle. It has six years of connected records and about 10 GB of data spread across 11 services:
Slack, Linear, Notion, HubSpot, Stripe, Google Calendar, PostHog, Google Analytics, Google Search Console, BigQuery, Snowflake

The tasks start mostly from one month of PageMantle Slack activity, but the evidence an agent needs often lives in the other ten services. An agent might have to write SQL against BigQuery or Snowflake to check a number someone threw out in a thread.

Each run goes like this. The agent gets a snapshot of the company at a fixed moment, the newest Slack messages, and one standing instruction: assess what is going on and help if it is useful. It can search and read across all 11 services. Then it picks one outcome: a channel message, a thread reply, a direct message to the right people, or nothing at all.

The controls are tight. Every model gets the same instructions, the same tools, the same company snapshot, high reasoning effort, and a budget of 180 seconds of model response time (tool time not counted). If a run hits the limit, it stops on the spot, and if help was needed and nothing went out, it scores as a miss.

Scoring is done by two LLM evaluators who don't know which model they're grading and don't see each other's verdicts. They grade 0 to 10 against a reference solution, with the company data and the full action log in hand, across four dimensions:
1. Intervention or silence: did it help where help was needed and hold back where it wasn't?
2. Content and evidence: were the conclusions accurate and backed by data it actually read?
3. Clarity and tone
4. Audience and location: right people, right channel, thread or DM?

There are 50 situations across eight task types: Find, Explain, Analyze, Verify, Diagnose, Decide, Coordinate and Guard.

The results

Score out of 10, cost per task, average time, average tool calls, and how many of the 10 "stay silent" tasks the model got right:
GPT-6 Astra: 8.97, $0.693, 54 s, 19.3 calls, silent 8/10
GPT-6.1 Sol: 8.65, $0.112, 54 s, 18.0 calls, silent 8/10
Claude Fable 5.2: 8.17, $1.87, 60 s, 20.9 calls, silent 6/10
Claude Opus 5.5: 7.84, $1.28, 29 s, 10.0 calls, silent 8/10
Claude Fable 5.1: 7.50, $3.02, 51 s, 14.5 calls, silent 6/10
Claude Sonnet 5.5: 6.65, $0.420, 15 s, 8.9 calls, silent 6/10
GPT-6 Luna: 6.38, $0.0070, 50 s, 13.7 calls, silent 4/10
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash: 6.35, $0.026, 86 s, 21.1 calls, silent 4/10
Mistral Large 4: 6.09, $0.082, 85 s, 22.5 calls, silent 4/10
Claude Haiku 5.5: 6.05, $0.075, 28 s, 12.1 calls, silent 5/10
Gemini 4 Argon: 5.60, $0.403, 164 s, 34.5 calls, silent 10/10
Grok 4.7: 4.51, $0.425, 145 s, 35.5 calls, silent 6/10

Check the 95% intervals before quoting the ranking. Astra is 8.30 to 9.52, Sol 7.88 to 9.31, Fable 5.2 7.34 to 8.89. Sol sits inside Astra's range and Fable inside Sol's, so the top three are a cluster with OpenAI slightly ahead.

Five things in the data that matter more than the ranking

1. Silence is the hard part, and quality filters won't save you 🤐

Every model is decent at helping. Holding back is what separates them. Even the best models spoke up in 2 of the 10 situations where silence was correct. Deepnote notes that those unnecessary messages were accurate, well written and correctly placed. The issue had already been handled.

So a second model that checks whether the message is good won't catch these. The message is good. It just shouldn't exist.

Deepnote draws a useful line between easy and hard silence. When the resolution is sitting in the same thread, every model holds back. When the thread looks open and there's a solid analysis on offer, nearly every model jumps in, even if the matter was closed somewhere else, like a Linear ticket or a DM.

2. Talking out of turn costs more, not just in noise

For the same model, speaking when it should have stayed quiet cost about 1.8x as much and took about 1.8x as long as staying quiet. So every false alarm is the most expensive outcome you can get: you pay for the full investigation and you annoy a human.

3. The Anthropic models split by working style

Fable 5.2 is third overall and leads the Decide task type (compare options, recommend a next step). It helped in 40 of 40 cases but held back in only 6 of 10. Opus 5.5 is the mirror image: slightly lower score, but 8 of 10 on silence, and it's the fastest of the leaders at 29 seconds with 10 tool calls on average.

Fable 5.2 makes roughly twice the tool calls in roughly twice the time of Opus 5.5 for a score about 4% higher. If your agent fires on every thread in a busy workspace, Opus's restraint and speed may be worth more to you than Fable's extra 0.33 points.

4. More tool calls did not mean better answers

The two models at the bottom made the most calls. Gemini 4 Argon averaged 34.5 calls and Grok 4.7 averaged 35.5. Both also burned most of the 180-second budget (164 s and 145 s on average) and helped in only 23 and 24 of the 40 tasks where help was needed. Deepnote says nearly every miss on helping was a run that hit the time limit before sending anything.

So read Gemini's perfect 10 of 10 on silence with care. It also failed to deliver help in 17 cases where help was needed.

5. Numbers are the common weak spot 📊

Analyze tasks ask the agent to pull figures from PostHog, BigQuery or Snowflake and check them against a claim someone made in Slack. That was the weakest task type for 8 of the 12 models. Verify, which checks a claim against a source document, was the opposite: nearly every model did well. Query, aggregate and compare is still where agents fall over.

The cost spread is the real engineering decision 💸

Sol scored 8.65 at $0.112 per task. Fable 5.2 scored 8.17 at $1.87. That's roughly 17x the cost for a lower score on this benchmark. GPT-6 Luna and Claude Fable 5.1 are about 430x apart in price ($0.0070 vs $3.02) but only 1.12 points apart in score.

Deepnote ran the math for an always-on agent that investigates about 2,500 threads a month:
Sol: $281 a month
Astra: $1,732 a month
Fable 5.2: $4,684 a month

Their recommendation is routing: send routine threads to a cheap, capable workhorse and escalate to a stronger model when there are numbers to reconcile, a decision to weigh, or a chance the matter is already closed. They're clear that they did not test a router. It's a design suggestion drawn from the score and cost spread, so measure it on your own traffic before you trust it.

What I would actually build from this

These are design choices, not benchmark results.

Make "is this already handled?" a separate, explicit step before the agent writes anything. Deepnote recommends exactly this. In practice it means the first tool calls should check for closure signals outside the thread: a linked ticket moved to done, a reply in a DM, a calendar event that already covers it, a recent Stripe refund for the customer being discussed. Only if those checks come back empty should the agent move on to analysis.

Split the decision from the writing. Run a cheap gate model that answers one question: speak, or stay silent, and why. Only call the expensive model when the gate says speak. Because a false alarm costs about 1.8x a correct silence, the cheapest win is killing unnecessary investigations early.

Track false alarms as their own metric. Most teams log "did the agent help?" and the answer is almost always yes. Log the rate at which humans reacted to a proactive message with nothing, a thumbs-down, or "already fixed." That's your silence score in production.

Treat numeric claims as a separate path. If a thread contains a number ("signups dropped 20% this week"), route it to whichever model handles SQL and analytics best in your own tests, and have the agent show the query it ran in the message. Analyze was the weakest task type for most models, so the query is the evidence.

Run it on your own agent

Everything is open. The code, documentation and tasks are Apache 2.0 on GitHub at https://t.co/OxPvIR7e4L, and the PageMantle dataset is CC BY 4.0 on Hugging Face. The tools run against a fixed local dataset, so no live accounts are needed, and the repo ships eight runnable examples, one per task type. Drop your own harness or router in and see if your silence check moves the number.

Limits worth knowing before you quote it

It's a 50-task panel, and each task type has only 5 to 8 tasks, so per-type rankings are tendencies, not facts. Deepnote says a larger task set is coming in the next version.

The snapshot is fixed. The agent doesn't choose when the test begins, and teammates don't reply, so it measures one contribution at one moment, not the effect on a team over weeks.

Every model ran at high effort. Lower or higher effort settings will move both score and cost, and those sweeps haven't been run yet.

The takeaway for anyone building agents that act without being asked: model choice moves your score by a point or two, but the design of the decision to speak is where your users will feel the difference. Build the silence check first, measure false alarms, and route the expensive model only to threads that earn it.

https://t.co/OxPvIR7e4L
